nameStory: The forget-me-not gets its romantic name from European folklore, where a knight picking these flowers for his beloved fell into a river and threw the bouquet to her, crying 'forget me not!' The 'strict' part of this species' name refers to its upright, rigid growth habit compared to other sprawling forget-me-nots.
description: Blue forget-me-not is a small annual wildflower that grows just 2-8 inches tall with a distinctly upright, unbranched stem. Its tiny sky-blue flowers have five rounded petals arranged around a bright yellow center, creating perfect little stars that seem almost too delicate to be real. The entire plant has a somewhat stiff, erect appearance and is covered in soft, fine hairs that give it a slightly fuzzy texture when you touch it.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright blue flowers, about 1/8 inch across, with five rounded petals and a distinctive yellow center that looks like a miniature sun - much smaller and more delicate than other forget-me-nots

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Distinctly upright and unbranched stem that feels quite rigid and stiff when gently touched, unlike the sprawling or branched stems of related species

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel soft and fuzzy due to tiny hairs covering the surface - run your finger along them for a velvety sensation

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny nutlets that develop where the flowers were, clustered tightly along the upper stem in a distinctive spiral pattern

habitat: Look for blue forget-me-not in sandy, disturbed soils and open areas like field edges, roadsides, and waste places throughout New England. It particularly favors well-drained, somewhat poor soils and thrives in areas with little competition from larger plants.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear in late spring, typically May through early June, creating tiny blue dots in open areas. The whole plant is most visible and identifiable during this blooming period.
seasonality.summer: Plants may continue flowering into early summer but often become less noticeable as they set seed. Seeds ripen and disperse by mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: As an annual, plants die back completely by fall, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the soil.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground plant parts remain visible - exists only as seeds waiting to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Despite producing some of the tiniest flowers in New England - barely bigger than the head of a pin - each blue forget-me-not plant can produce hundreds of these perfect miniature blossoms, creating what looks like a constellation of fallen stars scattered across the ground.
confusionNotes: Blue forget-me-not is easily confused with other forget-me-not species, but look for its distinctive stiff, unbranched stem and much smaller flowers. Water forget-me-not has larger flowers and grows near water, while wood forget-me-not is taller and more branched. Remember: 'strict and small' for this species.
contextualKnowledge: The alternate common name 'blue scorpion grass' comes from the way the flower clusters curl up like a scorpion's tail before blooming - this coiled arrangement is actually characteristic of the entire borage family, which includes familiar herbs like borage and comfrey.
compareHints: Blue forget-me-not is the most rigid and unbranched of all New England forget-me-nots, with distinctly smaller flowers than its relatives. Water forget-me-not spreads along streams with larger blooms, wood forget-me-not branches extensively and grows much taller, and field forget-me-not has a more sprawling habit with medium-sized flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Water forget-me-not is distinguished from other forget-me-not species by its preference for wet habitats and its perennial, mat-forming growth habit.
Wood forget-me-not differs from water forget-me-not by preferring drier woodland soils versus wet areas, and it has a more compact growth habit.
Field forget-me-not differs from water forget-me-not by preferring dry, disturbed soil rather than wet areas, and having more pronounced patent hairs on its stems.
Unlike the common water forget-me-not which stays bright blue and grows in wet areas, changing forget-me-not prefers drier disturbed soil and shows its telltale color progression.
Among New England's forget-me-nots, bay forget-me-not stands out for having the smallest flowers and most relaxed growth habit.
Among New England's forget-me-nots, early forget-me-not is the smallest and most easily overlooked.
